In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Surah al-Waqi'ah

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When the Inevitable Event occurs﴾ ﴿there will be no denying its occurrence﴾. What appears to me as correct is that "idhā" (when) here is the temporal particle that carries the meaning of a conditional, and that His subsequent saying: ﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 4] is a substitute (badal) for His saying: ﴿When the Inevitable Event occurs﴾, and that the response (jawab) of "idhā" is His saying: ﴿then the companions of the right hand﴾. This is the view chosen by Abu Hayyan, in contrast to those who claimed that it has been stripped of the meaning of a conditional here, and that it is governed by an implied "udhkur" (remember), or that it is a subject (mubtada'); and in contrast to those who claimed that it is governed by the "laysa" (there is not) mentioned after it.

The well-known position of the majority of grammarians is that "idhā" is a temporal adverb carrying the meaning of a conditional, governed by its response. On this basis, the meaning is: when the Resurrection comes and these tremendous states take place, the status of the companions of the right hand and the companions of the left hand will become manifest.

His saying in this noble verse: ﴿When the Inevitable Event occurs﴾ means: the Resurrection comes to pass. So "al-Waqi'ah" is one of the names of the Resurrection, like "al-Tammah" (the Overwhelming Calamity), "al-Sakhkhah" (the Deafening Blast), "al-Azifah" (the Approaching Hour), and "al-Qari'ah" (the Striking Calamity).

Indeed, He, exalted is He, has made clear that the Inevitable Event is the Resurrection in His saying: ﴿Then when the Trumpet is blown with a single blast, and the earth and the mountains are lifted and crushed with a single crush, then on that Day the Inevitable Event will occur, and the sky will be split open, for it will be frail on that Day﴾ [al-Haqqah: 13–16].

His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿there will be no denying its occurrence﴾ has several well-known interpretations among the scholars, all of which are true, and some of which are supported by the Qur'an.

The first interpretation: His saying "kadhibah" (denying) is a verbal noun (masdar) that came in the form of an active participle (ism al-fa'il), so "al-kadhibah" means "al-kadhib" (denial), just as "al-'afiyah" means "al-mu'afah" (well-being), and "al-'aqibah" means "al-'uqba" (the final outcome). From this usage is His saying, exalted is He, according to a number of scholars: ﴿You will not hear in it any idle talk﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 11]. They said: its meaning is "you will not hear in it any vain speech." According to this view, the meaning is: there is no falsehood or failure in the occurrence of the Resurrection; rather, it is a matter that certainly and inevitably happens.

(p-509)From this meaning is the saying of the Arabs: "The horseman charged at his opponent and did not deny (kadhaba)," meaning: he did not hold back, did not fail, and did not show cowardice.

And from it is the verse of Zuhayr:

A lion, fierce, hunting men, when the lion in fight withholds from his peers, he is truthful (sadaqa).

This meaning is indicated by many verses of the Book of Allah, such as:

• His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah, there is no god but He. He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt﴾ [al-Nisa': 87];

• His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it﴾ [al-Hajj: 7];

• His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, You are the gatherer of mankind for a Day about which there is no doubt﴾ [Al 'Imran: 9]. We have previously mentioned the verses clarifying this in Surah al-Shura, in discussing His saying: ﴿and warn of the Day of Assembly, about which there is no doubt﴾ [al-Shura: 7].

The second interpretation: the "lam" in His saying "li-waqi'atihā" is temporal (zarfiyyah), and "kadhibah" is an active participle functioning as an adjective of an implied noun, meaning: there is no soul in the occurrence of the Inevitable Event that is a liar; rather, all people on the Day of Resurrection are truthful in acknowledging the Resurrection and confirming it, and there is no soul among them that denies it by rejecting it or that declares it false.

This meaning is supported in general by verses of the Book of Allah, such as His saying: ﴿They will not believe in it until they see the painful punishment﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 201], and His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be in doubt about it until the Hour comes upon them suddenly or there comes upon them the punishment of a barren Day﴾ [al-Hajj: 55].

We have previously mentioned the verses clarifying this in Surah al-Naml, in discussing His saying: ﴿Rather, their knowledge of the Hereafter has failed. Rather, they are in doubt about it. Rather, they are blind to it﴾ [al-Naml: 66]. As for the remaining interpretations, the Qur'an may indicate its meaning, but in my view it is not free from remoteness, and therefore I have not mentioned it; and the closest of them in my view is the first.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Abasing [some], exalting [others]﴾.

It is the predicate (khabar, the part that completes the sentence) of a deleted subject (mubtada', the topic of the sentence), meaning: "It is abasing, exalting." The object of each of the two descriptive words is deleted.

Some scholars said: Its implied meaning is: it abases peoples into the depths of the Fire and exalts peoples to the high ranks, to Paradise. This meaning is indicated by many verses, such as:

• His words: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest level of the Fire﴾ [an-Nisa: 145];

• And His words, the Exalted: ﴿And whoever comes to Him as a believer, having done righteous deeds, for them are the high ranks﴾ ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, beneath which rivers flow﴾ [Ta-Ha: 75-76];

• And His words, the Exalted: ﴿And the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in distinction﴾ [al-Isra: 21].

Verses of this kind are many and well known.

Some scholars said: Its implied meaning is: it abases peoples who were elevated in this world, and exalts peoples who were humbled in this world. This meaning is supported by verses from the Book of Allah, the Exalted, such as His words: ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed﴾ ﴿And when they passed by them, they would wink at one another﴾ up to His words: ﴿So today, those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾ ﴿upon couches, looking on﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 29-35], along with other verses.

Some scholars said: Its implied meaning is: it abases some of the heavenly bodies that were high, like the stars that fall and scatter on the Day of Resurrection. That is a lowering of them after they were high, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And when the stars scatter﴾ [al-Infitar: 2], and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And when the stars are dimmed﴾ [at-Takwir: 2].

"Exalting" means: it raises some of the bodies that were low, like the mountains, which are lifted from their places and move between the sky and the earth, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And the Day We set the mountains in motion, and you see the earth laid bare﴾ [al-Kahf: 47]. His words ﴿and you see the earth laid bare﴾ mean that nothing of the mountains remains on its surface. And Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them fixed, while they pass as the clouds pass﴾ [an-Naml: 88].

We have already mentioned that the verified position indicated by the Qur'an is that this occurs on the Day of Resurrection, and that the mountains are moved between the sky and the earth like the movement of clouds, which are the rain-clouds.

He has also stated explicitly that the mountains and the earth will be carried on the Day of Resurrection, as in His words, the Exalted: ﴿And when the Trumpet is blown with one blast﴾ ﴿and the earth and the mountains are lifted and crushed with one blow﴾ [al-Haqqah: 13], and the verse continues.

According to this view, the purpose is to magnify the greatness of the Day of Resurrection, and that the order of the world will be thrown into disorder on it. According to the first two views, the purpose is encouragement and warning, so that people in this world fear the causes of lowering in the Hereafter and obey Allah, and desire the causes of elevation and obey Him as well. We have mentioned many times that the correct approach to such a matter is to take the verse as encompassing all of these meanings together.

God the Exalted says: ﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking﴾ ﴿and the mountains are crumbled into powder﴾ ﴿and become scattered dust﴾.

We have already mentioned that the more apparent view to us is that His words "When the earth is shaken" are a substitute (badal) for His words: ﴿When the Inevitable Event occurs﴾. Ar-Rajj means violent agitation. What this verse indicates, that on the Day of Resurrection the earth will be shaken violently, is made clear in other verses, such as His words: ﴿When the earth is shaken with its (final) earthquake﴾. We have already cited the verses that clarify this in the beginning of Surat al-Hajj, in the discussion of His words: ﴿Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing﴾ [al-Hajj 22:1]. As for His words "and the mountains are crumbled into powder" (bussat al-jibalu bassan), its meaning has several views among the scholars. These views are close to one another, none of them contradicts another, and all of them are true, and the Qur'an bears witness to each of them.

We have already mentioned, in the translation of this blessed Book, that a noble verse may have several views, all of which are true and all of which the Qur'an bears witness to. So we will mention all the views and their Qur'anic evidences.

The first view: Most of the exegetes (mufassirun) said: "the mountains are crumbled into powder" means they are pulverized into fine dust until they become like basisah, which is flour kneaded with ghee. From this is the saying of a thief from Ghatafan who wanted to bake some flour he had, but feared he would be hurried away from it, so he ordered his two companions to knead it so they could eat it as kneaded flour, and this is basisah:

*Do not bake bread and basabis, nor delay with a camel made to kneel and held back.*

This view is borne out by the Qur'an, such as His words: ﴿On the day when the earth and the mountains quake, and the mountains become a heap of loose sand﴾ [al-Muzzammil 73:14]. His words "a heap of loose sand" (kathiban mahilan) mean crumbling sand, and from this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*And a day on the back of the sand-dune, when she was unattainable to me and swore an oath that was not undone.*

The resemblance between kneaded flour and crumbling sand is clear. So His words "and the mountains became a heap of loose sand" agree in meaning with the explanation of "the mountains are crumbled into powder," since their crumbling is their pulverizing and grinding, as you see.

What these verses indicate, that the mountains will be stripped of the strength of stone and will, after firmness and strength, take on an extreme softness like that of fine flour and crumbling sand, is generally supported by their comparison in some verses to fluffed wool, which is the 'ihn, such as His words: ﴿And the mountains will be like fluffed wool﴾ [al-Qari'ah 101:5], and His words: ﴿On the day when the sky will be like molten brass, and the mountains will be like 'ihn﴾ [al-Ma'arij 70:8-9]. The root meaning of 'ihn is more specific than wool in general, because it is specifically dyed wool. From this is the saying of Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma in his Mu'allaqah (a celebrated pre-Islamic ode):

*As if the girls of dyed wool, at every halting place they alighted at, were the seeds of the fanna plant, unbroken.*

Some said: The mountains have streaks, white and red, with varied colors, and black ravens. So when they are crumbled and pulverized on the Day of Resurrection and scattered in the air, they resemble 'ihn when the wind scatters it in the air. This view is indicated by the arrangement of their becoming "scattered dust" with the particle fa' (then/so) after His words "and the mountains are crumbled into powder," because al-habaʾ is what descends through a window from the rays of the sun when it faces it:

*Munbathth* means scattered. Describing them as scattered dust is most fitting, since bass means crumbling and grinding.

The second view: the meaning of His words "and the mountains are crumbled into powder" is that they will be set in motion between the heaven and the earth. On this view, their bass means driving and moving them, from the saying of the Arabs: bassat al-ibil abussuha (I drove the camels), and absastuha ubussuha (I drove them), both dialectal forms meaning "I drove them." From this is the hadith: "People will go out from Madinah to Yemen, Syria and Iraq, driving (their camels), and Madinah is better for them, if only they knew."

This view is borne out by verses of the Book of Allah, such as His words: ﴿And the day We set the mountains in motion﴾ [al-Kahf 18:47], and His words: ﴿And the mountains will move, moving﴾ [at-Tur 52:10].

We have already cited the verses clarifying this in Surat an-Naml, in the discussion of His words: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them fixed, while they pass by like clouds﴾ [an-Naml 27:88].

The third view: the meaning of His words "and the mountains are crumbled into powder" is that they will be pulled from their places and uprooted. We have already made clear that this view returns to the first view, with full clarification of the states of the mountains on the Day of Resurrection and their stages, through Qur'anic verses. In Surat Ta-Ha, in the discussion of His words: ﴿They ask you about the mountains; say: My Lord will scatter them as dust﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:105]. As for His words in this noble verse, ﴿and they become scattered dust﴾, it is like His words: ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion, and they will become a mirage﴾ [an-Naba' 78:20]. Al-habaʾ, when it is scattered (inbatha), that is, dispersed, dissolved and becomes nothing; and as for the mirage (as-sarab), Allah the Exalted said about it: ﴿Until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing﴾ [an-Nur 24:39].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 56, verse 7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you became three kinds (azwajan thalathah)﴾.

That is: you became three kinds. The Arabs use kāna (to be) in the sense of ṣāra (to become), and from it is His saying: ﴿And do not approach this tree, lest you be among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35], that is, lest you become among the wrongdoers.

And from it is the saying of the poet:

"In a barren wilderness, the riding-camels seemed like the sandgrouse of al-Huzn, whose eggs had become chicks."

His saying, azwājan, means: kinds, three in number. Then He clarified these three kinds by His saying: ﴿So the companions of the right hand — what are the companions of the right hand? And the companions of the left hand — what are the companions of the left hand? And the foremost, the foremost. Those are the ones brought near, in gardens of delight﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 8–12]. As for the companions of the right hand (aṣḥāb al-maymanah), they are the companions of the right (aṣḥāb al-yamīn), as He made clear by His saying: ﴿And the companions of the right — what are the companions of the right? Among lote-trees without thorns﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 27–28]. And the companions of the left hand (aṣḥāb al-mash'amah) are the companions of the left, as He made clear by His saying: ﴿And the companions of the left — what are the companions of the left? In scorching wind and boiling water﴾, and the verses [al-Waqi'ah: 41–42].

Some scholars said: they were called companions of the right because they are given their books in their right hands.

It was also said: because they are led to the right, to Paradise.

It was also said: because they are on the right of their father Adam, as the Prophet ﷺ saw them thus on the night of the Isra' (Night Journey).

It was also said: they were called companions of the right and companions of the right hand because they are maymanīn (blessed), that is, blessed in themselves, because they obeyed their Lord and so entered Paradise; and al-yumn is blessing.

The others were called companions of the left. It was said: because they are given their books in their left hands.

It was also said: because they are led to the left, to the Fire. The Arabs call the left shu'm (ill omen) just as they call the right yumn (blessing). From here it was said of them: companions of the left (aṣḥāb al-mash'amah), or because they are mashā'īm (ill-omened) for themselves: they disobeyed God, so He caused them to enter the Fire. Al-mashā'īm is the opposite of al-maymānīn. And from it is the saying of the poet:

"Ill-omened ones, who do not reform their tribe, nor does any crow-caller call except with its separation."

He, exalted is He, clarified that the foremost are the ones brought near, and that is in His saying: ﴿And the foremost, the foremost. Those are the ones brought near﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 10–11]. These three kinds mentioned, and their recompense, are at the beginning of this noble surah, and their recompense also comes at its end, in His saying: ﴿As for if he is of those brought near, then rest and provision and a Garden of delight. And as for if he is of the companions of the right, then peace be upon you from the companions of the right. And as for if he is of the deniers, the astray, then a welcome of boiling water and burning in Hellfire﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 88–94].

The deniers are the companions of the left hand, and they are the companions of the left.

And He, exalted is He, mentioned some attributes of the companions of the right hand and the companions of the left hand in al-Balad, in His saying: ﴿Freeing a slave, or feeding on a day of hunger an orphan near of kin﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Those are the companions of the right hand. And those who disbelieved in Our signs, they are the companions of the left hand; over them is a fire closed in﴾ [al-Balad: 18–20].

His saying in this noble verse: ﴿What are the companions of the right hand?﴾ and His saying: ﴿What are the companions of the left hand?﴾ are interrogatives intended to express wonder at the state of these in happiness, and the state of those in wretchedness. The clause in both is a subject and predicate, and it is the predicate of the subject before it: the companions of the right hand in the first, and the companions of the left hand in the second.

This style is frequent in the Qur'an, such as: ﴿The Inevitable Reality — what is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 1–2], ﴿The Striking Calamity — what is the Striking Calamity?﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 1–2]. The link in the predicate clause in all the mentioned verses is the repetition of the subject's wording within the predicate clause, as is not hidden. His saying "and the foremost" does not mention in it an interrogative of wonder as He mentioned in what preceded it, but in its place He mentioned the repetition of the word "the foremost."

The more apparent view in its grammatical analysis is that it is a subject and predicate, according to the Arab practice of repeating the word and intending to inform about the second concerning the first, meaning that the word about which information is given is the well-known one whose predicate needs no definition. From it is the saying of Abu al-Najm:

"I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry is my poetry; by God, how excellent is my skill, what my breast conceals!"

His saying "wa-shi'ri shi'ri" means: my poetry is that whose report has reached you and whose description has come to you.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 56, verse 13:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿A multitude from among the earlier peoples﴾ ﴿and a few from among the later peoples﴾.

His saying "thullatun" (a multitude) is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the implied meaning is "they are a multitude." The "thullah" (multitude) is a group of people. Its original sense is a piece of something, and it is from "ath-thall," which means breaking.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Al-thullah" derives from "ath-thall," which means breaking, just as "al-ummah" (community) derives from "al-umm," which means a person's form or figure. It is as though it is a group that has been broken off from the people and cut off from them. End of quotation from him.

Know that "al-thullah" includes a large group. From this is the poet's saying:

"Then there came to them a Khindifi multitude, with an army like a foaming torrent of flood."

For his saying "a torrent of flood" indicates the large number of this army, which is referred to as a "thullah."

The people of knowledge have differed about what is meant by this "multitude" from the earlier peoples and this "few" from the later peoples mentioned here, just as they differed about the two multitudes mentioned in His saying: ﴿A multitude from among the earlier peoples﴾ ﴿and a multitude from among the later peoples﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 39-40]. Some people of knowledge said: all of these mentioned are from this Ummah, and the intended "earlier ones" among them are the Companions.

Some scholars also include with them the generations testified to as good in his saying (ﷺ): "The best of generations is my generation, then those who follow them," the hadith. Those who said that they are all from this Ummah said: the intended "few" is only ﴿and a multitude from among the later peoples﴾, and they are those after that until the Hour arrives.

Some scholars said: the intended "earlier ones" in both places are the nations that passed before this Ummah, and the intended "later ones" in both places are this Ummah.

The one who narrows this (its ruling), may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The apparent meaning of the Qur'an in this context is that the "earlier ones" in both places are from the past nations, and the "later ones" in both places are from this Ummah, and that His saying the Exalted: ﴿A multitude from among the earlier peoples﴾ ﴿and a few from among the later peoples﴾ refers to the foremost (al-sabiqun) only, and that His saying: ﴿A multitude from among the earlier peoples﴾ ﴿and a multitude from among the later peoples﴾ refers to the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin) only.

We say that this is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an regarding the three matters: that the verses encompass all nations, that the "few from among the later peoples" is specifically among the foremost, and that the "multitude from among the later peoples" is specifically among the companions of the right, because this is clear from the context of the verses.

As for the verses encompassing all nations, the beginning of the surah indicates it, because His saying: ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and it becomes scattered dust﴾ undoubtedly does not single out one nation over another, and that all are equal in the terrors, the reckoning, and the recompense.

This indicates that His saying: ﴿And you will be in three categories﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 7] is general to all the people of the gathering. It becomes clear that the foremost and the companions of the right include those who are from the past nations, and among them are those who are from this Ummah.

Based on this, the apparent meaning of the Qur'an is that the foremost from the past nations are more numerous than the foremost from this Ummah, and that the companions of the right from the past nations are not more numerous than the companions of the right from this Ummah, because He expressed about the foremost of this Ummah with His saying: ﴿and a few from among the later peoples﴾, and expressed about the companions of the right of this Ummah as ﴿and a multitude from among the later peoples﴾.

There is nothing strange in this, because the past nations are many nations, and among them are many prophets and messengers. There is no barrier to the foremost of them from Adam to Muhammad (ﷺ) gathering more than the foremost of this Ummah alone.

As for the companions of the right from this Ummah, it is possible that they are more numerous than the companions of the right from all the nations, because "thullah" encompasses a large number, and one of two large numbers may be more than the other, even though both are large.

For this reason, you know that what the apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates and what Ibn Jarir chose does not contradict what has come that half of the people of Paradise are from this Ummah.

As for the claim that His saying: ﴿and a few from among the later peoples﴾ indicates, by the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, that it refers specifically to the foremost, this is because Allah said: ﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾ ﴿those are the ones brought near﴾ ﴿in the Gardens of Pleasure﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 10-12], then He said, the Exalted, informing about these foremost who are brought near: ﴿A multitude from among the earlier peoples﴾ ﴿and a few from among the later peoples﴾.

As for the claim that His saying: ﴿and a multitude from among the later peoples﴾ refers specifically to the companions of the right, this is because Allah the Exalted said: ﴿We have made them virgins﴾ ﴿loving, of equal age﴾ ﴿for the companions of the right﴾ ﴿a multitude from among the earlier peoples﴾ ﴿and a multitude from among the later peoples﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 36-40]. The meaning is: they, that is the companions of the right, are a multitude from the earlier peoples and a multitude from the later peoples, and this is clear, as you see.
